comparedAgainst: GeeksforGeeks, Big O Notation (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/analysis-algorithms-big-o-analysis/): gives the c/n0 definition, simplification rules and a table of classes with code snippets; no measurements, no case where the notation misleads, no worked witness proofs.

freeCodeCamp, What is Big O Notation Explained (https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/big-o-notation-why-it-matters-and-why-it-doesnt-1674cfa8a23c/): definition, Omega/Theta, a selection-sort derivation and a 'why it doesn't matter' section that only asserts quicksort beating merge sort in practice; no reproducible measurement.
Sources spot-checked, not competitors: NIST DADS big-O entry, Sedgewick and Wayne section 1.4, Microsoft Learn Array.Sort, dotnet/runtime ArraySortHelper.cs (all fetched and read).
justification: Judged as a Google low-value-content reviewer, this page is not thin, not padded and not copied. It clearly out-delivers the two ranking pages it was compared with: those give the definition and a class table, while this article derives the step counts itself, produces worked (c, n0) witnesses including a disproof and exercises, and measures a real insertion-vs-merge sort crossover in C#, plus the effect of a compiler flag and a tuned hybrid cutoff. That is original, checkable value. Spot-checks passed: the NIST definition (constants c and k, and the note that Big-O is often misused to mean 'equal to'), the Sedgewick and Wayne quote on caching, garbage collection and JIT, the Array.Sort remarks (16-element insertion sort, heapsort fallback, O(n log n)) and the 2- and 3-element special cases in ArraySortHelper.cs all match what the article says. The stated CPU (i7-11700K) matches this machine. Web searches for the article's distinctive phrasing and its 3n+40 / c=4 / n0=40 example found no copy; the 'age 30 is under 90' analogy is a common teaching image, used here in the article's own words. The opening delivers a concrete scenario, there is no filler intro or 'key takeaways' outro, headings are content-specific, and exercise forms vary (produce a witness, true/false/not-a-claim, extend the code, nested-loop bound). Points held back from a higher score: (1) the docs/crosslinks file the brief relies on does not exist, and the body has no link to the published binary-search or arrays articles, so the page leaves the reader few next steps and ends inside an exercise solution; (2) the sorts are printed twice (in the collapsed full program and again as a snippet), which reads as padding; (3) a few claims rest on runs whose output the reader never sees (the no-Optimize run, the 80,000-lap row), so they are trusted rather than verifiable; (4) small unsupported or loose statements (table row 'O(log n) gains one step', 'O(n!) grows faster still', causal explanation of insertion sort's small constants asserted rather than shown); (5) a mild house-style fingerprint shared with siblings ('on the machine used here/for this page', scenario-first openings, 'X does not move Y' contrasts). None is a policy risk; together they keep it at MDN/Real Python-with-nits, not clearly better than the best result.
